title: Iran War Underscores the Diverging Aims of Trump and Netanyahu
partialText: The United States views Iran through a prism of global responsibilities and strategic goals. Israel has a more regional approach. After nearly three weeks of war, their paths are diverging.

title: Deferring to Trump, G.O.P. Lawmakers Resist a Public Accounting on Iran
partialText: Nearly three weeks into a war that polls show is unpopular, top Republicans have yet to call administration officials to testify about it, arguing that hearings would put divisions on display.

title: Spain Says the Sun Shields It From Rising Gas Costs. Is That True?
partialText: Pedro Sánchez, Spain’s prime minister, said the nation’s renewable energy system has softened the financial fallout from the war in Iran. The story is more complex.

title: U.S. Prosecutors Investigate Colombia’s President, a Onetime Trump Foe
partialText: The Justice Department is examining whether President Gustavo Petro of Colombia has ties to drug traffickers.

title: Trump Administration Sues Harvard Over Accusations of Antisemitism
partialText: The administration had spent months investigating the Ivy League school. The two sides had been in talks to negotiate a settlement.

title: Fed Official Urges Caution on Rate Cuts as Iran War Drags On
partialText: Christopher J. Waller, a Federal Reserve governor, said he would support rate cuts later this year if the labor market continued to weaken.

title: Trump Friend Asked ICE to Detain the Mother of His Child
partialText: Paolo Zampolli, a former modeling agent and a longtime Trump ally, was in a custody battle over his son. An ICE official agreed to help.

title: Pregnant in ICE Detention: Handcuffs and Pleas for Medical Care
partialText: Women describe conditions that violate longstanding agency guidelines for how pregnant detainees should be treated.

title: New Data Shows Where ICE Has Been Most Active This Year
partialText: The pace of ICE arrests nationwide has topped 1,100 per day on average in 2026, but the rate of arrests has varied across the country in sometimes surprising ways.

title: ICE Released Hundreds of Children from Immigration Detention
partialText: About 50 children were in federal detention in Dilley, Texas this week, down from about 500 in January. It is unclear how many were deported, but some are back at their U.S. schools.

title: Chuck Norris, Action Star of ‘Walker, Texas Ranger,’ Dies at 86
partialText: He channeled his martial arts skills into heroic roles in films like “The Delta Force” and “Missing in Action” and in the long-running TV series “Walker, Texas Ranger.”

title: Cesar Chavez Avenue May Soon Be Gone. Yet to Be Confronted: His Legacy.
partialText: After the revelations of sex abuse, the public is left to make sense of the labor leader’s work and life.

title: How a Civil Rights Icon Used His Power to Abuse Girls and Women
partialText: For five years, our reporters Manny Fernandez and Sarah Hurtes followed allegations that the civil rights icon Cesar Chavez had sexually abused girls and women at all levels of the United Farm Workers movement. Manny Fernandez takes us inside their investigation.

title: Cesar Chavez, a Civil Rights Icon, Is Accused of Abusing Girls for Years
partialText: An investigation by The New York Times found extensive evidence that the United Farm Workers co-founder groomed and sexually abused girls who worked in the movement.

title: How a Stickup Man Became a Sought-After Jailhouse Lawyer
partialText: Obsessed with proving his innocence, Quentin Lewis devoted years in isolation to learning the law. Now he is taking on his captors in prison tribunals.

title: BTS Is Back With ‘Arirang,’ but the K-Pop Landscape Has Changed
partialText: The superstar boy band returns after a four-year hiatus on Friday. The genre it helped turn into a global juggernaut has endured some shifts, and minted new stars.

title: What To Know About the BTS Comeback Concert Streaming Live on Netflix
partialText: The K-pop supergroup’s first show in over three years will stream live on Netflix at 7 a.m. Eastern time on Saturday. The New York Times will cover it live from Seoul.

title: A.I. Is Writing Fiction. Publishers Are Unprepared.
partialText: Book publishing has few safeguards in place to prevent the unwitting publication of a novel heavily generated by artificial intelligence.

title: Blood Plasma Centers Move Into More Middle-Class Neighborhoods
partialText: Across the United States, plasma centers are opening in wealthier areas as more people struggle with the high cost of housing, groceries and health care.

title: Record Number of Student Loan Borrowers Are in Delinquency and Default
partialText: Recently released data from the Education Department showed that by the end of last year, 7.7 million borrowers had defaulted on $181 billion in federal student loans.

title: How New Mexico Became an Obamacare Success Story
partialText: Affordable Care Act enrollment has dropped across the United States since the enhanced federal subsidies expired. But New Mexico has record numbers of people signing up.

title: CBS News Cuts 6% of Staff as Bari Weiss Reshapes the Division
partialText: The layoffs affected several dozen employees at the news division, which is owned by the technology heir David Ellison. The company is also shuttering CBS News Radio.

title: Can Jonah Peretti Save BuzzFeed From Extinction?
partialText: Facing financial straits, the founder is betting on a skunkworks for A.I. experiments.

title: How Muslim Businesses in New York Prepare to Celebrate Eid
partialText: From Fordham to Bay Ridge to Hollis, Muslim businesses get ready for Eid al-Fitr, the exultant celebration marking the end of the holy month of Ramadan.

title: Supreme Court Allows Street Preacher’s Lawsuit
partialText: Gabriel Olivier was arrested after violating an ordinance restricting demonstrations outside an amphitheater in Brandon, Miss.

title: Boston Scientific Knew of Pacemaker Battery Problems for Years
partialText: Boston Scientific announced multiple recalls but has said its battery issues were limited. One internal test in 2025 found batteries with an “extremely high failure rate.”

title: What the ‘Project Hail Mary’ Directors Learned From a Firing
partialText: Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, best known for animations like the “Spider-Verse” films, took lessons from “Solo: A Star Wars Story,” a project from which they were dismissed.

title: ‘Project Hail Mary’ Review: Ryan Gosling Is Lost and Found in Space
partialText: The actor plays a molecular biologist trying to help save the world in this upbeat science-fiction fantasy from Phil Lord and Christopher Miller.

title: Andy Weir on Writing the Hit Book Behind the Movie ‘Project Hail Mary’
partialText: The author talked about adapting his best-selling novel for film, creating the beloved character Rocky and making complex science feel approachable.

title: We’re All Living in the ‘Mirror World’ Now
partialText: Naomi Klein and Ezra Klein discuss what the success of MAGA reveals about the American left.

title: Whose War?
partialText: We look at the diverging goals of the U.S. and Israel in the war on Iran.

title: Late Night Pans Trump’s Pearl Harbor Joke
partialText: “Let me tell you: There is no doubt in my mind that everything he knows about Pearl Harbor begins and ends with a movie starring Ben Affleck,” Jimmy Kimmel said.

title: Seeking to Rely Less on China, U.S. Pushes a Rare Earths Partnership on a Reluctant Brazil
partialText: Seeking to reduce its reliance on China, the United States is pushing for a critical minerals deal with Brazil. The South American country is less eager.

title: Lukashenko Jailed Her in Belarus, but She Wants the World to Talk to Him
partialText: Maria Kalesnikava is campaigning for the West to engage with the regime in Belarus that imprisoned her for more than five years.

title: Calvin Tomkins, Who Profiled Giants of Modern Art, Dies at 100
partialText: On the staff of The New Yorker for more than 60 years, he wrote about Duchamp, Rauschenberg and many others. His books include “Living Well Is the Best Revenge.”

title: New Spider Mimics ‘The Last of Us’ Zombie Fungus Cordyceps
partialText: A newly discovered species of spider in the Ecuadorean Amazon mimics a pathogen, known as a zombie fungus, to protect itself.
